questions.prompt: Which of these expressions evaluate to true? Select all that apply.
options: null == undefined
NaN == NaN
null == 0
questions.explanation: null == undefined is true by a special rule, and '' coerces to the number 0 so '' == 0 is true. null == 0 is false because null only loosely equals undefined, and NaN is never equal to anything, including itself.

questions.prompt: Which of these values are falsy? Select all that apply.
options: NaN
0n (the BigInt zero)
'0' (a string containing a zero)
[] (an empty array)
new Boolean(false)
questions.explanation: 0n and NaN are falsy. '0' is a non-empty string, [] is an object, and new Boolean(false) is an object too, so all three are truthy.

questions.prompt: Which statements about JavaScript numbers are correct? Select all that apply.
options: typeof 10n is 'bigint'
1n + 1 evaluates to 2n
Math.trunc(-4.5) is -4 while Math.floor(-4.5) is -5
Integers beyond Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER cannot always be represented exactly as a Number
questions.explanation: trunc drops the fraction while floor rounds toward negative infinity, integers past 2^53 - 1 lose precision, and BigInt has its own typeof. Mixing BigInt and Number in arithmetic such as 1n + 1 throws a TypeError.

questions.prompt: Which statements about hoisting are correct? Select all that apply.
options: A function expression assigned to a const can be called before the assignment line
Reading a let variable inside its temporal dead zone yields undefined
A function declaration can be called before its position in the source
Reading a var variable before its assignment yields undefined
questions.explanation: Function declarations are hoisted with their body and var bindings start as undefined. A const holding a function expression and a let variable in the TDZ both throw a ReferenceError if accessed early.

questions.prompt: Which statements about closures are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Each call to the outer function creates a fresh set of captured variables
In for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++), each iteration gets its own binding of i
A closure stores a snapshot copy of captured primitive values at creation time
A closure can read and update variables of its enclosing scope after the outer function has returned
In for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) with setTimeout callbacks, each callback sees its own value of i
questions.explanation: Closures capture variables, not value snapshots, and every outer call makes new ones. let creates a per-iteration binding, but with var all callbacks share one i and typically see its final value.

questions.prompt: Which statements about call, apply and bind are correct? Select all that apply.
options: bind invokes the function immediately and returns its result
apply takes its arguments as a single array-like object while call takes them individually
A function returned by bind keeps its bound this even if you later use call on it with another object
apply only works if you pass a real Array instance, not an array-like object
questions.explanation: apply accepts any array-like, and a bound function's this cannot be overridden by call or another bind. bind does not invoke the function; it returns a new function.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Object.freeze and Object.seal are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Object.seal still allows changing the values of existing writable properties
In strict mode, assigning to a property of a frozen object silently does nothing
Object.freeze prevents adding, deleting and reassigning own properties of that object
Object.freeze makes nested objects immutable as well
questions.explanation: freeze blocks add, delete and reassign, while seal blocks add and delete but allows writes to writable properties. Both are shallow, and strict mode throws a TypeError on a failed write to a frozen object instead of failing silently.

questions.prompt: Which statements about copying objects are correct? Select all that apply.
options: structuredClone throws a DataCloneError when the value contains a function
structuredClone preserves the class prototype of an instance
JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x)) keeps Date values as Date objects
The spread expression {...obj} creates a deep copy
structuredClone can copy Map, Set and Date instances
questions.explanation: structuredClone handles Map, Set and Date and throws on functions. Spread is shallow, structuredClone returns plain objects without the original prototype, and the JSON round trip turns Dates into strings.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Promise combinators are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Promise.any rejects as soon as the first input promise rejects
Promise.all rejects as soon as any input promise rejects
Promise.all cancels the remaining pending operations when one input rejects
Promise.allSettled resolves with an array of objects having status 'fulfilled' or 'rejected'
Promise.race ignores rejected promises and waits for the first fulfilled one
questions.explanation: all rejects fast and allSettled reports every outcome. any waits for the first fulfillment, race settles with the first settled promise whatever its outcome, and nothing is cancelled because promises have no cancellation.

questions.prompt: Which statements about async/await are correct? Select all that apply.
options: An async function always returns a promise, even when it returns a plain value
await can be used in any regular function as long as it sits inside a try block
A try/catch around a promise-returning call catches its rejection even if the call is not awaited
A throw inside an async function rejects the returned promise instead of throwing synchronously to the caller
questions.explanation: Async functions wrap return values and thrown errors into a promise. await needs an async function (or a module top level), and without await a try/catch cannot see the later rejection.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Node.js timers and scheduling are correct? Select all that apply.
options: queueMicrotask schedules a callback on the microtask queue
setImmediate callbacks run in the timers phase
Inside an I/O callback, setImmediate always runs before a setTimeout with 0 delay
From the main module, the order of setTimeout(fn, 0) and setImmediate(fn) is always deterministic
questions.explanation: After an I/O callback the loop moves to the check phase before timers, so setImmediate wins. From the main module the order depends on process timing, setImmediate belongs to the check phase, and queueMicrotask uses the microtask queue.

questions.prompt: Which statements about iterables and iterators are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Iterating a Map with for...of yields only its values by default
Plain objects are iterable with for...of by default
Any object with a [Symbol.iterator]() method that returns an iterator can be used with for...of and spread
Strings are iterable and iterate by code point
Array destructuring such as const [a, b] = x uses the iterator protocol
questions.explanation: for...of, spread and array destructuring all use Symbol.iterator, and strings iterate by code point. Plain objects have no default iterator, and a Map yields [key, value] entries by default.

questions.prompt: Which statements about ES modules in Node.js are correct? Select all that apply.
options: In an ES module Node defines __dirname and __filename just like in CommonJS
Top-level await is allowed in ES modules
require() is a global in ES modules, available in the same way as in CommonJS
Import bindings in ES modules are live views of the exporting module's variables
questions.explanation: ESM bindings are live and top-level await works in modules. __dirname, __filename and require are CommonJS wrapper variables that are not defined in ES modules (use import.meta or createRequire).

questions.prompt: Which statements about type aliases and interfaces in TypeScript are correct? Select all that apply.
options: An interface can be declared directly as a union of other types
Two interfaces with the same name in the same scope are merged
A type alias can name a union type such as string | number
Two type aliases with the same name in the same scope are merged
questions.explanation: Interfaces support declaration merging and aliases can name unions. Interfaces cannot be unions, and duplicate type alias names are a compile error instead of merging.

questions.prompt: Which statements about TypeScript utility types are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Pick<T, K> requires K to be assignable to keyof T
ReturnType<typeof fn> yields the return type of fn
Partial<T> makes every property of T optional
Required<T> makes every property of T readonly
Omit<T, K> requires K to be assignable to keyof T
questions.explanation: Partial, Pick and ReturnType behave as described. Required removes optionality (Readonly adds readonly), and Omit's K is only constrained to keyof any, so it does not error for keys missing from T.

questions.prompt: Which statements about the libuv thread pool in Node.js are correct? Select all that apply.
options: The default thread pool size is 4
Callbacks for finished thread-pool tasks run on the pool's worker threads
Asynchronous fs operations are executed on the thread pool
dns.lookup uses the thread pool because it calls getaddrinfo
Network socket reads and writes are executed on the thread pool
questions.explanation: The default UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE is 4, and fs and dns.lookup work run there. Sockets use non-blocking OS polling instead, and completion callbacks always run on the main event loop thread.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Node.js streams are correct? Select all that apply.
options: writable.write() returning false signals that the buffer reached highWaterMark and the producer should wait for 'drain'
stream.pipeline() propagates errors and destroys the streams it connects
A Transform stream is a kind of Duplex stream
pipe() automatically destroys every stream in the chain when one of them errors
questions.explanation: write() returning false is the back-pressure signal, pipeline() handles error propagation and cleanup, and Transform extends Duplex. pipe() does not clean up the other streams when one errors, which is why pipeline() exists.

questions.prompt: Which statements about worker_threads, child_process and cluster are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Worker threads can share memory through SharedArrayBuffer
cluster workers run inside the primary process and share its heap
child_process.fork() starts a separate Node.js process with its own V8 instance
Worker threads run on the same event loop as the main thread
questions.explanation: Workers can share SharedArrayBuffer memory, and fork() creates a separate process. cluster workers are separate processes, and each worker thread has its own event loop and V8 isolate.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Express middleware are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Error-handling middleware must be registered before the routes it handles
Error-handling middleware is identified by having four parameters (err, req, res, next)
In Express 4, a rejected promise returned by an async handler is automatically forwarded to error middleware
A middleware that neither calls next() nor sends a response leaves the request hanging
questions.explanation: The four-argument signature marks error middleware, and forgetting next() or a response hangs the request. Express 4 does not catch async rejections (Express 5 does), and error middleware goes after the routes.

questions.prompt: Which statements about graceful shutdown of a Node.js HTTP server are correct? Select all that apply.
options: server.close() forcibly terminates requests that are still in progress
A process.on('SIGKILL') handler can run cleanup code before the process dies
On SIGTERM, a server should stop accepting new connections and let in-flight requests finish before exiting
server.close() stops the server from accepting new connections
questions.explanation: The standard flow is to stop accepting new connections with close() and drain in-flight work. close() does not abort active requests, and SIGKILL cannot be caught or handled.

questions.prompt: Which statements about the complexity of JavaScript built-ins are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Array.prototype.unshift on a large array is O(1)
Set.prototype.has is O(1) on average
Array.prototype.indexOf is O(log n) because it uses binary search
Array.prototype.includes is O(n)
questions.explanation: includes and indexOf scan linearly, and Set lookup is hash based so it is O(1) on average. unshift must move existing elements so it is O(n), and indexOf never assumes the array is sorted.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Map versus plain objects as hash tables in JavaScript are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Map keys can be objects, compared by reference
Plain object keys are converted to strings (unless they are symbols)
A plain {} literal has no inherited properties, so obj['toString'] is undefined
Map exposes its entry count through the size property
questions.explanation: Map accepts any key type, plain objects coerce keys to strings, and Map has a size property. A plain object literal inherits from Object.prototype, so toString is defined; use Object.create(null) or a Map to avoid that.

questions.prompt: Which statements about sorting algorithms are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Counting sort is comparison based, so it cannot beat O(n log n)
Insertion sort takes O(n) time on an already sorted array
Merge sort can be implemented as a stable sort
Quicksort with a fixed pivot choice has an O(n log n) worst case
Merge sort runs in O(n log n) time in the worst case
questions.explanation: Merge sort is O(n log n) in the worst case and stable, and insertion sort is O(n) on sorted input. Quicksort degrades to O(n^2) with bad pivots, and counting sort avoids comparisons entirely.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Array.prototype.sort in JavaScript are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Since ES2019 the sort is required to be stable
sort returns a new array and leaves the original unchanged
Without a comparator, elements are compared as strings
A comparator returning a boolean such as (a, b) => a > b is a reliable way to sort numbers
questions.explanation: The default order is by string value, so [10, 9, 1] sorts as 1, 10, 9, and ES2019 requires stability. Comparators must return a negative, zero or positive number, and sort mutates in place (toSorted is the copying version).

questions.prompt: Which statements about binary tree traversals are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Inorder traversal of a binary search tree visits keys in ascending order
An iterative preorder traversal can use an explicit stack
A recursive traversal uses call stack space proportional to the tree height
Postorder visits a node before its children
questions.explanation: Inorder on a BST is sorted, iterative DFS uses a stack, and recursion depth equals tree height. Postorder visits children first and the node last.

questions.prompt: Which statements about binary heaps are correct? Select all that apply.
options: The array backing a binary heap is fully sorted
Reading the minimum of a min-heap is O(1)
JavaScript's standard library has a built-in PriorityQueue class
A heap can be built from n elements in O(n) time using bottom-up heapify
Insert and extract-min on a binary heap are O(log n)
questions.explanation: Heap push and pop are O(log n), peek is O(1) and bottom-up heapify is O(n). A heap is only partially ordered by the heap property, and JavaScript has no built-in priority queue.

questions.prompt: Which statements about topological sorting are correct? Select all that apply.
options: If Kahn's algorithm outputs fewer than V nodes, the graph contains a cycle
A DAG has exactly one valid topological ordering
A topological ordering exists only for directed acyclic graphs
Kahn's algorithm repeatedly removes nodes whose in-degree is zero
questions.explanation: Only DAGs have topological orders, and Kahn's algorithm peels off zero in-degree nodes; leftover nodes mean a cycle. A DAG usually has many valid orderings, not exactly one.

questions.prompt: Which statements about shortest-path and spanning-tree algorithms are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Dijkstra with a binary heap runs in O(V + E) time
Prim's algorithm cannot be implemented with a heap
Kruskal's algorithm sorts the edges and uses union-find to skip edges that would form a cycle
Dijkstra's algorithm requires non-negative edge weights to be correct
Bellman-Ford can detect negative cycles reachable from the source
questions.explanation: Dijkstra needs non-negative weights, Bellman-Ford detects negative cycles, and Kruskal pairs sorted edges with union-find. Dijkstra with a binary heap is O((V + E) log V), and Prim commonly uses a heap.

questions.prompt: Which statements about bit manipulation in JavaScript are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Bitwise operators on Numbers convert their operands to 32-bit signed integers
x >>> 0 converts a value to an unsigned 32-bit integer
x & (x - 1) clears the lowest set bit of x
1 << 31 evaluates to a positive number
questions.explanation: JS bitwise operators work on 32-bit signed ints, >>> 0 reinterprets as unsigned, and x & (x - 1) drops the lowest set bit. 1 << 31 sets the sign bit and gives -2147483648.

questions.prompt: Which statements about encapsulation in JavaScript and TypeScript are correct? Select all that apply.
options: TypeScript's private keyword prevents access at runtime
Fields declared with a # prefix cannot be accessed outside the class body
Private # fields appear in Object.keys(instance)
A closure can hide state so that only the returned functions can reach it
questions.explanation: # fields and closures give real runtime privacy. TypeScript's private keyword is erased at compile time, and # fields are not listed by Object.keys.

questions.prompt: Which statements about composition and inheritance are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Composition requires the composed objects to share a common base class
Composition models a has-a relationship while inheritance models an is-a relationship
JavaScript lets a class extend several classes at once with extends A, B
Deep inheritance hierarchies make base-class changes risky for subclasses (fragile base class)
questions.explanation: Has-a versus is-a is the core distinction, and deep hierarchies create fragile-base-class problems. JS allows only a single extends target, and composition needs no shared base class.

questions.prompt: Which statements about the Liskov Substitution Principle are correct? Select all that apply.
options: A subclass that strengthens a method's preconditions violates LSP
Square extending Rectangle with coupled width and height setters is a classic LSP violation
Code satisfies LSP as long as the subclass type-checks
Objects of a subtype should be usable wherever the base type is expected without breaking correctness
questions.explanation: LSP is about behavioural substitutability, and strengthened preconditions or the Square/Rectangle setter coupling break it. Type-checking alone proves nothing about behaviour.

questions.prompt: Which statements about the Dependency Inversion Principle and dependency injection are correct? Select all that apply.
options: High-level modules should depend on abstractions rather than on concrete low-level modules
Dependency injection and the Dependency Inversion Principle mean exactly the same thing
Constructor injection makes it easy to swap in a test double
The Dependency Inversion Principle requires using a DI container library
questions.explanation: DIP says to depend on abstractions, and constructor injection is one way to supply them and enables test doubles. DIP is a principle, DI is a technique, and no container is required.

questions.prompt: Which statements about the Singleton pattern in Node.js are correct? Select all that apply.
options: The module cache guarantees one instance even when two different copies of the same package exist in node_modules
Exporting an instance from a module gives a per-process singleton because Node caches modules
A singleton makes unit testing easier because global state stays isolated
Worker threads and cluster workers each get their own module instance
questions.explanation: Node caches a module per resolved file path within a process, so each process or worker thread gets its own instance. Duplicate package copies yield separate singletons, and global state generally hurts testability.

questions.prompt: Which statements about the Observer pattern with Node's EventEmitter are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Observers that are never unsubscribed can keep objects alive and cause leaks
Listeners added with on() are removed automatically after emit finishes
Emitting 'error' with no 'error' listener throws the error
A listener registered with once() is removed after its first invocation
questions.explanation: An unhandled 'error' event throws, once() auto-removes, and lingering listeners retain their closures. on() listeners stay registered until you remove them.

questions.prompt: Which statements about designing a Parking Lot in an LLD interview are correct? Select all that apply.
options: A Ticket entity linking vehicle, spot and entry time lets the exit fee be computed
Spot assignment should be safe against two vehicles claiming the same spot when state is shared
One ParkingLot class should own spot allocation, ticketing, pricing and payment to keep the design simple
Pricing rules are a good candidate for the Strategy pattern
questions.explanation: Strategy for pricing, a Ticket entity and safe spot allocation are standard good design points. Putting everything in one class violates single responsibility and makes the design hard to extend.

questions.prompt: In JavaScript, the expression 0 ?? 'default' evaluates to 'default'.
questions.explanation: The nullish coalescing operator only falls through for null and undefined, so 0 ?? 'default' returns 0. It is the || operator that would return 'default' because 0 is falsy.

questions.prompt: Variables declared with let are not hoisted at all, which is why reading them before the declaration throws a ReferenceError.
questions.explanation: let and const bindings are hoisted to the top of their block but stay uninitialised until the declaration runs. That gap is the temporal dead zone and it is what causes the ReferenceError.

questions.prompt: A subclass method can read a parent class's private field by writing this.#x, provided the instance was created through the subclass.
questions.explanation: Private names are lexically scoped to the class body that declares them, so this.#x in a subclass is a SyntaxError unless the subclass declares #x itself. The parent must expose the value through a method or accessor.

questions.prompt: If a .catch() handler returns a normal value without throwing, the promise returned by that .catch() call is fulfilled with that value.
questions.explanation: A handler that returns normally recovers the chain, so the promise from .catch() fulfills with the returned value and later .then callbacks run. It only stays rejected if the handler throws or returns a rejected promise.

questions.prompt: A chain of microtasks that keeps scheduling new microtasks can prevent setTimeout callbacks from ever running.
questions.explanation: The microtask queue is drained completely before the event loop moves to the next macrotask, so microtasks that endlessly enqueue more microtasks starve timers and I/O.

questions.prompt: Code in an ES module runs in strict mode by default, without a 'use strict' directive.
questions.explanation: ES modules are always strict mode code, so things like assigning to an undeclared variable throw and this at the top level is undefined.

questions.prompt: The TypeScript compiler verifies that a user-defined type guard with return type 'x is string' actually performs a correct string check.
questions.explanation: A type predicate is trusted by the compiler and its body is not checked against the claim. A wrong guard silently produces incorrect narrowing and unsound code.

questions.prompt: In TypeScript, a variable holding an object with extra properties can be passed to a parameter typed as an interface with fewer properties, because assignability is structural.
questions.explanation: Structural typing only requires the needed members to be present. Excess property checks apply only to fresh object literals written directly at the call site, not to variables.

questions.prompt: A value of type unknown can be assigned to a variable of type any without a type assertion or narrowing.
questions.explanation: unknown is assignable only to unknown and any, and any accepts every value. Assigning unknown to any type such as string requires narrowing or an assertion.

questions.prompt: The Node.js event loop is implemented by the V8 engine.
questions.explanation: V8 executes JavaScript, while the event loop and asynchronous I/O are provided by libuv. Node's bindings connect the two.

questions.prompt: A fast salted SHA-256 hash is as suitable for storing passwords as bcrypt, because both are one-way functions.
questions.explanation: Password hashing should be deliberately slow and tunable to resist brute force, as bcrypt, scrypt and Argon2 are. A fast hash lets attackers test enormous numbers of guesses per second, even with a salt.

questions.prompt: A rate limiter that keeps its counters in process memory enforces a single shared limit across several Node instances running behind a load balancer.
questions.explanation: Each process has its own memory and counters, so the effective limit multiplies with the number of instances. A shared store such as Redis or a database is needed for a global limit.

questions.prompt: An algorithm whose running time is O(n) is also O(n^2), because Big-O only states an upper bound.
questions.explanation: Big-O is an asymptotic upper bound, so any function bounded by n is also bounded by n^2. Big-Theta is the notation that states a tight bound.

questions.prompt: After O(n) preprocessing into a prefix-sum array, the sum of any subarray can be answered in O(1) time.
questions.explanation: With prefix[i] holding the sum of the first i elements, the sum of a range is prefix[r + 1] - prefix[l], a constant-time subtraction.

questions.prompt: Naive recursive Fibonacci, where fib(n) calls fib(n - 1) and fib(n - 2) with no memoization, runs in linear time.
questions.explanation: The two recursive calls overlap heavily and the call tree grows exponentially, roughly O(phi^n). Memoization reduces it to O(n).

questions.prompt: To validate a binary search tree, it is enough to check that each node's left child is smaller and its right child is larger than that node.
questions.explanation: The BST property applies to every node in a subtree, not just direct children. A node deep in the left subtree can still be larger than an ancestor, so you must track min and max bounds or compare inorder values.

questions.prompt: Finding the k largest of n numbers with a min-heap capped at size k takes O(n log k) time.
questions.explanation: Each of the n elements causes at most one push and one pop on a heap of size k, costing O(log k) each, so the total is O(n log k).

questions.prompt: Plain BFS with a queue finds the cheapest path in a graph whose edges have different positive weights.
questions.explanation: BFS minimises the number of edges, not total weight, so it is only correct for unweighted graphs. Weighted graphs with non-negative weights need Dijkstra's algorithm.

questions.prompt: A subclass method that throws for inputs the base class method accepts breaks the Liskov Substitution Principle.
questions.explanation: Callers written against the base type expect those inputs to work, so a subclass that rejects them is not safely substitutable and violates the behavioural contract.

questions.prompt: EventEmitter.emit() invokes the registered listeners synchronously, in the order they were registered.
questions.explanation: emit() calls each listener directly and waits for it to return before the next, so listeners run in registration order before emit returns. Any asynchrony has to be added by the listener itself.

questions.prompt: A transaction runs under PostgreSQL's default isolation level (READ COMMITTED) with no explicit locking. Which anomalies can it experience? Select all that apply.
options: Dirty read of another transaction's uncommitted row
Non-repeatable read of a row it read earlier
Phantom rows appearing when a range query is repeated
Lost update from an application-level read-then-write cycle
questions.explanation: Postgres never exposes uncommitted data at any level, so dirty read is wrong. At READ COMMITTED each statement gets a fresh snapshot, so non-repeatable reads, phantoms and read-modify-write lost updates are all possible.

questions.prompt: Which statements about default isolation behaviour in PostgreSQL and MySQL InnoDB are correct? Select all that apply.
options: PostgreSQL's default isolation level is READ COMMITTED.
InnoDB's default isolation level is SERIALIZABLE.
InnoDB's default isolation level is REPEATABLE READ.
PostgreSQL treats a READ UNCOMMITTED request as READ COMMITTED.
PostgreSQL's REPEATABLE READ allows phantom reads because it only protects rows already read.
questions.explanation: Postgres defaults to READ COMMITTED and maps READ UNCOMMITTED to it; InnoDB defaults to REPEATABLE READ, not SERIALIZABLE. Postgres REPEATABLE READ is snapshot isolation, so phantoms do not appear in its snapshot (option 5 is wrong).

questions.prompt: Which statements about precedence graphs for testing conflict serializability are correct? Select all that apply.
options: A schedule is conflict serializable if and only if its precedence graph has no cycle.
Two reads of the same item by different transactions create an edge between them.
An edge Ti to Tj means a conflicting operation of Ti comes before one of Tj on the same item.
A cycle proves the schedule is not conflict serializable, though it might still be view serializable.
An acyclic graph means the schedule is already a serial schedule.
questions.explanation: Acyclic means conflict serializable and edges come from ordered conflicting operations. Read-read pairs do not conflict (option 2 wrong), and an acyclic graph only means the schedule is equivalent to some serial one, not that it is serial (option 5 wrong).

questions.prompt: Which statements about strict two-phase locking (strict 2PL) are correct? Select all that apply.
options: It guarantees conflict-serializable schedules.
It holds exclusive locks until the transaction commits or aborts.
It makes deadlocks impossible.
It prevents cascading aborts.
It lets a transaction acquire new locks after it has released some.
questions.explanation: Holding exclusive locks to commit keeps others from reading uncommitted data, so there are no cascading aborts, and 2PL yields conflict serializability. Deadlocks are still possible (option 3 wrong), and acquiring locks after releasing violates the two-phase rule (option 5 wrong).

questions.prompt: Which statements about the timestamp-based wait-die and wound-wait deadlock prevention schemes are correct? Select all that apply.
options: A transaction aborted by either scheme restarts with a brand-new timestamp.
In wait-die, an older transaction requesting a lock held by a younger one waits.
In wound-wait, an older transaction requesting a lock held by a younger one aborts the younger one.
Neither scheme allows a cycle of waiting transactions to form.
questions.explanation: Wait-die lets older wait and kills younger requesters; wound-wait lets older preempt (wound) younger holders. Both avoid wait cycles. A restarted transaction keeps its ORIGINAL timestamp so it eventually becomes oldest and cannot starve (option 1 wrong).

questions.prompt: Which statements about MVCC in PostgreSQL are correct? Select all that apply.
options: An UPDATE overwrites the row in place and copies the old value to an undo log.
An UPDATE writes a new row version and leaves the old version for concurrent snapshots.
VACUUM reclaims dead row versions that no snapshot can still see.
A long-running open transaction has no effect on what VACUUM can remove.
Plain reads do not block writers, and writers do not block plain reads.
questions.explanation: Postgres keeps old versions in the heap and VACUUM cleans them up. In-place update with an undo log describes InnoDB/Oracle, not Postgres (option 1 wrong). An old open transaction holds back the xmin horizon so VACUUM cannot remove versions it might still need (option 4 wrong).

questions.prompt: A table has a B-tree index on (a, b, c). Assuming no skip-scan optimisation, which predicates can use the index to seek on its leading columns? Select all that apply.
options: WHERE c = 3
WHERE a = 1
WHERE a = 1 AND b = 2
WHERE a = 1 AND b = 2 AND c = 3
WHERE b = 2 AND c = 3
questions.explanation: The leftmost-prefix rule: a seek needs a constraint on the leading column(s), so a, (a,b) and (a,b,c) work. Predicates on c alone or on (b,c) skip the leading column a, so they cannot be used for a seek.

questions.prompt: In which situations can adding a secondary index hurt a workload? Select all that apply.
options: Write-heavy tables, because every insert or update of an indexed column must also maintain the index.
Read-only primary key lookups, because extra indexes always make point reads slower.
A boolean column where almost all rows share one value, since the planner will often prefer a sequential scan anyway.
Memory-constrained servers, since index pages compete with table pages for the buffer pool.
questions.explanation: Indexes cost write work, memory and space, and low-selectivity indexes are rarely used. Extra indexes do not slow point reads that the planner serves from the primary key, so option 2 is wrong.

questions.prompt: Which statements about clustered and secondary indexes are correct? Select all that apply.
options: A table can have only one clustered index because rows can be physically ordered only one way.
In PostgreSQL, the CLUSTER command keeps the table sorted as new rows are inserted.
In InnoDB, secondary index entries store the primary key value, so a lookup may need a second B+ tree traversal.
In InnoDB, the leaf pages of the primary key index hold the full row data.
questions.explanation: InnoDB tables are clustered on the primary key and secondary indexes point back via the PK. Postgres CLUSTER is a one-time physical reorder and is not maintained for later inserts, so option 2 is wrong.

questions.prompt: Which statements about NULL in standard SQL are correct? Select all that apply.
options: NULL = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN, not TRUE.
COUNT(*) skips rows in which any column is NULL.
x NOT IN (subquery) returns no rows if the subquery produces a NULL.
AVG(col) ignores NULL values when computing the average.
WHERE col <> 5 returns rows where col is NULL.
questions.explanation: Comparisons with NULL yield UNKNOWN, so NOT IN against a list containing NULL can never be TRUE, and aggregates like AVG skip NULLs. COUNT(*) counts every row (option 2 wrong), and NULL <> 5 is UNKNOWN so such rows are filtered out (option 5 wrong).

questions.prompt: Which statements about SQL joins are correct? Select all that apply.
options: A CROSS JOIN of tables with m and n rows returns m * n rows.
Filtering a right-table column with WHERE r.x = 5 after a LEFT JOIN removes the NULL-extended rows, so it behaves like an INNER JOIN.
MySQL supports FULL OUTER JOIN natively.
INNER JOIN keeps left rows that have no match.
Joining on a non-unique column can return more rows than either input table.
questions.explanation: A cross join is a Cartesian product, a WHERE on the right table rejects NULL-extended rows, and duplicate matches multiply rows. MySQL has no native FULL OUTER JOIN (emulated with UNION), and INNER JOIN drops unmatched rows.

questions.prompt: Which statements about SQL window functions are correct? Select all that apply.
options: RANK leaves gaps in the numbering after tied rows.
DENSE_RANK leaves gaps in the numbering after tied rows.
ROW_NUMBER gives distinct numbers even to rows that tie on the ORDER BY.
Window functions collapse each partition into a single output row, like GROUP BY.
LAG returns a value from a preceding row within the partition ordering.
questions.explanation: RANK skips numbers after ties, ROW_NUMBER is always unique, and LAG reads an earlier row. DENSE_RANK has no gaps (option 2 wrong), and window functions keep every input row rather than collapsing them (option 4 wrong).

questions.prompt: Which statements about normal forms are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Every relation in BCNF is also in 3NF.
BCNF decomposition always preserves all functional dependencies.
2NF removes partial dependencies of non-prime attributes on part of a candidate key.
3NF removes multivalued dependencies.
A lossless, dependency-preserving decomposition into 3NF always exists.
questions.explanation: BCNF is stricter than 3NF, 2NF removes partial dependencies, and 3NF synthesis is lossless and dependency preserving. BCNF may lose dependencies (option 2 wrong), and multivalued dependencies are handled by 4NF, not 3NF (option 4 wrong).

questions.prompt: Which statements about OFFSET versus keyset pagination are correct? Select all that apply.
options: OFFSET N makes the database walk past and discard N rows before returning results.
Keyset pagination can jump straight to page 500 without knowing the previous page's last row.
Keyset pagination needs a deterministic, unique sort key, for example created_at plus id as a tie-breaker.
OFFSET pages never skip or repeat rows when new rows are inserted during paging.
Keyset pagination with an index on the sort key stays fast on deep pages.
questions.explanation: OFFSET cost grows with depth, while keyset seeks via an index from the last seen key and needs a unique ordering. Keyset cannot jump to an arbitrary page (option 2 wrong), and OFFSET shifts when rows are inserted, causing skips or repeats (option 4 wrong).

questions.prompt: Which statements about two-phase commit (2PC) are correct? Select all that apply.
options: A participant that voted YES must wait for the coordinator's decision and cannot safely abort on its own.
If the coordinator crashes after collecting votes, participants can finish by timing out and aborting unilaterally.
The coordinator must durably log its commit or abort decision so it can recover.
When 2PC completes, either all participants commit or all abort.
questions.explanation: After voting YES a participant is in doubt: it may already be committed elsewhere, so it blocks until the coordinator (or a log) tells it the outcome. Unilateral abort after YES can break atomicity, so option 2 is wrong.

questions.prompt: Which statements about page replacement algorithms are correct? Select all that apply.
options: FIFO replacement can exhibit Belady's anomaly, where more frames cause more page faults.
LRU can exhibit Belady's anomaly.
Optimal (MIN) cannot be implemented in a general-purpose OS because it needs knowledge of future references.
The Clock algorithm approximates LRU using a per-page reference bit.
questions.explanation: Belady's anomaly is a FIFO property; LRU and Optimal are stack algorithms and never show it (option 2 wrong). Optimal is only a benchmark since it needs future knowledge, and Clock gives a cheap LRU approximation via the reference bit.

questions.prompt: Which statements about thrashing and the working set are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Thrashing means a process spends more time swapping pages than executing.
Admitting more processes to raise CPU utilisation while the system is already thrashing can make things worse.
Thrashing is fixed by installing a faster CPU.
The working-set model keeps each process's recently referenced pages resident and suspends processes if total demand exceeds memory.
Thrashing occurs only with FIFO replacement.
questions.explanation: Thrashing is paging overhead dominating, and over-admitting processes deepens it, which the working-set model avoids by limiting multiprogramming. A faster CPU does not reduce page faults (option 3 wrong), and any replacement policy can thrash (option 5 wrong).

questions.prompt: Which statements about the TLB and multi-level page tables are correct? Select all that apply.
options: A TLB miss always raises a page fault.
Without address-space IDs (ASIDs/PCIDs), switching to another process's address space typically requires flushing the TLB.
Multi-level page tables save memory by allocating inner tables only for regions actually in use.
Larger pages (huge pages) increase how much memory a fixed-size TLB can cover.
The TLB stores the contents of recently used memory pages.
questions.explanation: A TLB miss just triggers a page-table walk; a page fault happens only if the mapping is invalid or the page is not resident (option 1 wrong). The TLB caches address translations, not page contents (option 5 wrong).

questions.prompt: Which statements about the Banker's algorithm are correct? Select all that apply.
options: A safe state is one in which some ordering of processes lets every process finish.
An unsafe state always means deadlock has already occurred.
Each process must declare its maximum resource needs in advance.
The Banker's algorithm detects deadlocks after they happen.
A request is granted only if the resulting state is safe.
questions.explanation: The Banker's algorithm is deadlock avoidance: it needs declared maximums and only grants requests that keep the system safe. Unsafe means deadlock is possible, not certain (option 2 wrong), and it avoids rather than detects deadlock (option 4 wrong).

questions.prompt: Which of the following are among the four conditions that must all hold simultaneously for a resource deadlock to occur? Select all that apply.
options: Mutual exclusion
Priority inversion
Hold and wait
No preemption
Circular wait
Starvation of a low-priority process
questions.explanation: The Coffman conditions are mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait. Priority inversion and starvation are separate scheduling problems, not deadlock conditions.

questions.prompt: Which statements about round robin and multilevel feedback queue (MLFQ) scheduling are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Round robin with a very large time quantum behaves like FCFS.
Round robin can starve a process indefinitely.
A very small quantum increases context-switch overhead.
MLFQ without a periodic priority boost can starve long CPU-bound jobs.
Round robin always gives lower average turnaround time than FCFS.
questions.explanation: A huge quantum means each process runs to completion, a tiny quantum wastes time switching, and MLFQ can starve demoted jobs without a boost. Round robin is starvation-free (option 2 wrong), and its average turnaround is often worse than FCFS for similar-length jobs (option 5 wrong).

questions.prompt: Which statements about FCFS, SJF and priority scheduling are correct? Select all that apply.
options: FCFS can cause the convoy effect when a long job runs ahead of many short jobs.
For jobs all available at time 0, SJF minimises average waiting time.
Priority scheduling cannot starve low-priority processes.
SJF is easy to implement exactly because the next CPU burst length is known.
SJF can starve long jobs when short jobs keep arriving.
questions.explanation: Convoy effect, SJF optimality for a simultaneous batch, and SJF starvation are all standard results. Priority scheduling can starve low-priority work unless aging is used (option 3 wrong), and burst length is unknown in practice and must be estimated (option 4 wrong).

questions.prompt: Which statements about condition variables and monitors are correct? Select all that apply.
options: pthread_cond_wait atomically releases the mutex and blocks, then re-acquires the mutex before returning.
A waiter should re-check its predicate in a while loop because of spurious wakeups and competing consumers.
A signal sent when no thread is waiting is remembered and wakes the next thread that calls wait.
A monitor bundles shared data with mutual exclusion over its procedures and condition variables.
questions.explanation: Wait must release the lock atomically to avoid lost wakeups, and predicates must be re-checked in a loop. Condition variables have no stored count, so a signal with no waiter is lost (option 3 wrong), unlike a semaphore.

questions.prompt: Which statements about file system journaling are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Journaling lets the file system replay or discard logged operations after a crash instead of scanning everything with fsck.
With journaling, data written by an application without fsync is guaranteed durable after a crash.
In ordered mode, only metadata is journaled, with data blocks written before the metadata commit.
The journal record is written before the in-place update (write-ahead).
questions.explanation: Journaling gives crash consistency of file system structures through write-ahead logging, with quick recovery. It does not make unsynced application data durable, so applications still need fsync (option 2 wrong).

questions.prompt: Which statements about inodes and links on a Unix-like file system are correct? Select all that apply.
options: An inode stores the file's name.
Directory entries map names to inode numbers.
Hard links are several directory entries pointing to the same inode.
Deleting one of two hard links to a file immediately frees its data blocks.
An inode holds metadata such as owner, permissions, size and pointers to data blocks.
questions.explanation: Names live in directory entries, which point to inodes that hold metadata and block pointers. Data is freed only when the link count reaches zero and no process has the file open, so option 4 is wrong; the name is not in the inode (option 1 wrong).

questions.prompt: Which statements about TCP and UDP are correct? Select all that apply.
options: TCP opens a connection with SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK.
UDP delivers datagrams in the order they were sent.
TCP preserves application message boundaries, so one send() always matches one recv().
TCP flow control uses the receiver's advertised window to avoid overrunning its buffer.
questions.explanation: TCP uses a three-way handshake and a receive window for flow control. UDP gives no ordering guarantee (option 2 wrong), and TCP is a byte stream with no message boundaries (option 3 wrong).

questions.prompt: Which statements about HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 are correct? Select all that apply.
options: HTTP/3 runs over QUIC, which is built on UDP.
HTTP/2 eliminates head-of-line blocking at every layer.
HTTP/2 multiplexes many streams over one connection.
HTTP/2 still suffers TCP-level head-of-line blocking when a packet is lost.
questions.explanation: HTTP/2 multiplexes streams but they share one TCP byte stream, so a lost packet stalls all of them. HTTP/3 moves to QUIC over UDP to remove that. HTTP/2 does not remove blocking at every layer (option 2 wrong).

questions.prompt: Which statements about the TLS handshake and certificates are correct? Select all that apply.
options: The client validates the server certificate chain up to a trusted root CA.
Application data is encrypted directly with the server's public key.
TLS 1.3 uses ephemeral (EC)DHE key exchange, which gives forward secrecy.
The server proves it holds the private key matching its certificate during the handshake.
questions.explanation: The client checks the chain and the server proves key possession by signing handshake data; ephemeral DH gives forward secrecy. Bulk data is encrypted with symmetric session keys derived from the handshake, not the server's public key (option 2 wrong).

questions.prompt: Which statements about WebSockets, Server-Sent Events (SSE) and long polling are correct? Select all that apply.
options: A WebSocket starts as an HTTP request that is upgraded to a full-duplex connection.
SSE lets the client push messages back to the server over the same stream.
SSE carries data only from server to client over HTTP.
In long polling, the server holds the request open until data is available or a timeout occurs.
questions.explanation: WebSocket upgrades from HTTP to a two-way channel, SSE is one-way server push, and long polling holds requests open. SSE cannot carry client-to-server messages on its stream; clients send those with separate requests (option 2 wrong).

questions.prompt: Which statements about REST and HTTP semantics are correct? Select all that apply.
options: PUT is idempotent: repeating the same request leaves the same server state.
POST is idempotent by definition.
401 means the caller is authenticated but not permitted.
GET is safe: it should not change server state.
201 Created with a Location header suits successful resource creation.
questions.explanation: PUT is idempotent, GET is safe, and 201 plus Location is the usual creation response. POST is neither safe nor idempotent (option 2 wrong), and 401 means missing or invalid authentication, while 403 means authenticated but forbidden (option 3 wrong).

questions.prompt: Which statements about idempotency keys on an API such as a payment endpoint are correct? Select all that apply.
options: The server stores the key with the outcome and returns the same response for a retry.
Each retry of the same operation should use a fresh key.
Reusing a key with a different request body should be rejected.
They matter mainly for non-idempotent requests such as POST, where a network retry could duplicate side effects.
They are needed for GET requests.
questions.explanation: The client sends one key per logical operation, reused across retries, and the server replays the stored result and rejects mismatched payloads. A fresh key per retry defeats the purpose (option 2 wrong), and GET is already safe and idempotent (option 5 wrong).

questions.prompt: Which statements about sessions and JWTs are correct? Select all that apply.
options: A stateless JWT stays valid until it expires unless the server keeps a denylist or similar state.
The payload of a signed JWT is encrypted, so clients cannot read it.
Server-side session records can be revoked immediately by deleting them.
Short-lived access tokens with refresh tokens limit the damage of a stolen token.
questions.explanation: Stateless tokens trade revocability for scalability, so short lifetimes and refresh tokens are used, while server sessions can be deleted at once. A signed JWT (JWS) is only base64url-encoded and anyone can read the payload (option 2 wrong).

questions.prompt: Which defences correctly address the named web vulnerability? Select all that apply.
options: CSRF: serving the site over HTTPS only.
CSRF: SameSite cookies and anti-CSRF tokens.
Stored XSS: a CORS policy on the API.
SSRF: allow-listing outbound destinations and blocking internal address ranges.
XSS: context-aware output encoding of untrusted data.
questions.explanation: SameSite and CSRF tokens block forged cross-site requests, allow-listing limits SSRF targets, and output encoding stops injected markup running. HTTPS does not stop CSRF, and CORS controls cross-origin reads, not script injection.

questions.prompt: Which statements about message delivery semantics are correct? Select all that apply.
options: At-least-once delivery can redeliver a message, so consumers should be idempotent.
At-most-once delivery never loses a message.
Effectively-once processing is typically built from at-least-once delivery plus idempotent or transactional handling.
At-least-once delivery guarantees there are no duplicates.
questions.explanation: At-least-once means retries can create duplicates, so consumers deduplicate, which is how effectively-once is usually achieved. At-most-once can drop messages (option 2 wrong), and at-least-once does not rule out duplicates (option 4 wrong).

questions.prompt: Which statements about Kafka are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Kafka deletes a message as soon as every consumer group has read it.
Kafka guarantees ordering only within a single partition.
If a consumer group has more consumers than partitions, the extra consumers sit idle.
Messages with different keys always go to the same partition.
Within one consumer group, a partition is assigned to at most one consumer at a time.
questions.explanation: Ordering is per partition, and a group assigns each partition to one member, so surplus consumers idle. Kafka retains messages by time or size, not by consumption (option 1 wrong), and different keys usually hash to different partitions (option 4 wrong).

questions.prompt: Which statements about caching strategies are correct? Select all that apply.
options: In cache-aside, the application reads the cache first and loads from the database on a miss.
Write-through lowers write latency compared with writing only to the database.
Write-back can lose acknowledged writes if the cache node fails before flushing.
Write-through keeps the cache and database in step, at the cost of write latency.
questions.explanation: Cache-aside is application-driven, write-back risks loss before flush, and write-through pays extra latency for consistency. Write-through adds a cache write on top of the database write, so it cannot lower write latency (option 2 wrong).

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL at REPEATABLE READ, a transaction that tries to update a row changed by another transaction that committed after its snapshot was taken fails with a serialization error.
questions.explanation: Postgres REPEATABLE READ is snapshot isolation with first-updater-wins, so the update raises SQLSTATE 40001 (could not serialize access) and the application must retry. This prevents lost updates, unlike READ COMMITTED.

questions.prompt: Optimistic locking with a version column works by including the version the row had when read in the UPDATE's WHERE clause and treating zero affected rows as a conflict.
questions.explanation: UPDATE ... SET ..., version = version + 1 WHERE id = ? AND version = ? succeeds only if nobody changed the row in between. Zero rows updated means a concurrent write won, and the app should reload and retry or report the conflict.

questions.prompt: In an LSM tree, writes are first recorded in a write-ahead log and an in-memory memtable, and the memtable is later flushed as an immutable sorted SSTable.
questions.explanation: LSM storage turns random writes into sequential ones: the WAL gives durability, the memtable buffers sorted data, and flushed SSTables are merged by background compaction.

questions.prompt: A PostgreSQL unique partial index created with a WHERE clause enforces uniqueness across every row of the table.
questions.explanation: A partial unique index only constrains rows satisfying its predicate. For example, UNIQUE (email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL allows duplicate emails among soft-deleted rows.

questions.prompt: To get the second highest distinct salary, filtering ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) = 2 is always correct, even when two employees share the top salary.
questions.explanation: ROW_NUMBER numbers tied rows distinctly, so if two people share the top salary, row 2 is the top salary again. DENSE_RANK() = 2 (or a distinct-salary subquery) gives the second highest distinct value.

questions.prompt: A PostgreSQL materialized view is automatically updated whenever its base tables change.
questions.explanation: A materialized view stores its results physically and stays stale until REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW is run (optionally CONCURRENTLY, which needs a unique index). A regular view is the one that always reflects current data.

questions.prompt: Decomposing relation R into R1 and R2 is lossless if the attributes common to R1 and R2 form a superkey of R1 or of R2.
questions.explanation: This is the standard test for a binary decomposition: if R1 intersect R2 functionally determines all of R1 or all of R2, a natural join of the parts reconstructs R exactly, with no spurious tuples.

questions.prompt: According to the CAP theorem, a system with no network partition must still give up either consistency or availability.
questions.explanation: CAP only forces the C-versus-A choice while a partition is happening. Without a partition both are achievable; the ongoing trade-off then is latency versus consistency, which is what PACELC adds.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually executes the statement, so running it on an UPDATE modifies data unless it is wrapped in a transaction that is rolled back.
questions.explanation: Plain EXPLAIN only plans, but EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the query to collect real timings and row counts, including side effects. Use BEGIN; EXPLAIN ANALYZE ...; ROLLBACK; to inspect writes safely.

questions.prompt: On Linux, a context switch between two threads of the same process avoids switching page tables, so it is generally cheaper than a switch between threads of different processes.
questions.explanation: Threads in one process share an address space, so the kernel keeps the same page tables and the TLB entries stay valid. Switching to another process changes the address space, which costs more and may flush TLB entries.

questions.prompt: Under demand paging, when a process touches a valid page that is not yet in memory, the kernel terminates it with SIGSEGV.
questions.explanation: That is a valid page fault: the kernel loads the page from disk or the page cache, updates the page table and resumes the instruction. SIGSEGV is sent only when the access is to an invalid address or violates permissions.

questions.prompt: On Linux, epoll lets one thread watch many sockets and returns only the descriptors that are ready, avoiding the per-call scan over every descriptor that select and poll need.
questions.explanation: epoll keeps the interest list in the kernel and reports ready events, so cost scales with active descriptors rather than total watched ones. That is why event-loop servers like Node.js handle many idle connections cheaply.

questions.prompt: Linux containers each run their own guest kernel, which is why they start faster than virtual machines.
questions.explanation: Containers share the host kernel and are isolated with namespaces and cgroups. VMs run separate guest kernels behind a hypervisor, which is why containers start faster but offer weaker isolation if the shared kernel is compromised.

questions.prompt: Calling access() to check permissions and then open() on the same path is vulnerable to a TOCTOU race, because the path can be replaced with a symlink between the two calls.
questions.explanation: The check and the use are not atomic, so an attacker can swap the file between them and make a privileged process open something else. Safer code opens first and then checks the resulting file descriptor, for example with fstat.

questions.prompt: A stack canary prevents a stack buffer overflow from overwriting the saved return address.
questions.explanation: Canaries do not stop the overflow; they detect it. The function checks the canary value before returning and aborts if it was overwritten, so the corrupted return address is never used, but nearby data may still be corrupted.

questions.prompt: A DNS CNAME record can coexist with other record types, such as MX, at the same name.
questions.explanation: A CNAME says the name is an alias for another name, so no other record types may exist at that name. This is why a CNAME cannot be placed at the zone apex, where SOA and NS records already exist.

questions.prompt: Adding a new optional field to a JSON response is generally considered a backward-compatible API change.
questions.explanation: Well-behaved clients ignore unknown fields, so additive changes do not need a new version. Removing or renaming fields, changing types or making request fields required are the breaking changes that need versioning.

questions.prompt: GraphQL eliminates the N+1 query problem by design, because the client fetches everything in a single request.
questions.explanation: One client request can still trigger one resolver call per item, and each of those may hit the database separately. Server-side batching such as DataLoader, or join-aware resolvers, is needed to avoid N+1.

questions.prompt: In OAuth 2.0, an access token proves the user's identity to the client application, so OpenID Connect is not needed for login.
questions.explanation: An OAuth access token grants delegated access to an API and is meant for the resource server, not as proof of who the user is. OpenID Connect adds the ID token and userinfo endpoint to authenticate users.

questions.prompt: With consistent hashing, adding one node to a ring of N nodes remaps only about 1/(N+1) of the keys on average, unlike hash(key) mod N, which remaps most keys.
questions.explanation: On a ring, a new node takes over only the key ranges adjacent to its positions, about its fair share of keys. With modulo hashing, changing N changes nearly every key's assignment, causing mass cache misses or data movement.
